params.question: A forensic physician classifies a wound in the MLC as 'incised'. Which of the following best explains the medico-legal significance of this classification?

answers.text: It confirms the wound was inflicted during a robbery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wound classification identifies the weapon class, not the circumstances of infliction. The MLC records factual findings; the investigation establishes the narrative.

answers.text: It indicates a sharp-edged weapon was used, narrowing the type of weapon the investigation must seek

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An incised wound — with clean margins, no tissue bridges, and length greater than depth — implies a sharp-edged weapon. This medico-legal opinion guides the investigation by narrowing the weapon class the police must recover.

answers.text: It determines the exact weapon used in the assault

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wound classification identifies the class of weapon (sharp-edged), not the specific weapon. Multiple weapons — knife, razor, glass shard — can all produce incised wounds.

answers.text: It establishes whether the injury was ante-mortem or post-mortem

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ante-mortem versus post-mortem distinction depends on vital reaction signs such as haemorrhage and inflammation, not on wound classification alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinction: wound classification tells you the class of weapon (sharp-edged vs blunt), not the specific weapon, circumstances, or timing of injury.
Wound classification is the foundational medico-legal opinion — it connects the wound morphology to a weapon class and directly influences the statutory charge.

params.question: At autopsy, a fractured femur shows organised granulation tissue bridging the fracture gap with early cartilage formation, but the X-ray shows no calcification. Which stage of fracture healing does this represent, and what is the approximate age of the fracture?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In the haematoma stage (24–48 hours), blood fills the fracture gap but organised granulation tissue has not yet formed. The X-ray shows only the fracture line.

Correct. Organised granulation tissue with early cartilage but no calcification characterises the soft callus stage, placing the fracture at approximately 2–6 weeks — a key forensic reference for dating disputed injuries.
The hard callus stage shows calcification visible on X-ray as woven bone replaces the cartilage. The absence of calcification in this case rules it out.
Remodelling shows mature lamellar bone replacing woven bone, with the fracture line becoming indistinct on X-ray — a much later appearance than described here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four stages: haematoma (24–48 h, no tissue organisation), soft callus (2–6 wk, granulation + cartilage, no calcification), hard callus (6–12 wk, calcification visible), remodelling (months, lamellar bone).
Matching histological and radiological findings to the correct healing stage is essential for forensically dating fractures when the history is unavailable or disputed.

params.question: During examination, you find an injury with intact overlying skin and subcutaneous haemorrhage that reproduces the outline of a cylindrical object. The injury was not visible on initial presentation but became apparent 36 hours later. What is the correct identification and key medico-legal inference?

answers.text: Abrasion — superficial scraping by a rough surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Abrasions involve only the epidermis and are visible immediately as the surface is scraped away. Intact overlying skin with deep haemorrhage points to a contusion.

answers.text: Laceration — torn tissue with tissue bridges from blunt force

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lacerations show torn, irregular wound edges with tissue bridges and disrupted skin. Here the skin is intact, which rules out any wound that breaches the surface.

answers.text: Contusion — patterned bruising from a cylindrical blunt weapon; delayed visibility is characteristic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A contusion shows haemorrhage beneath intact skin. Patterned contusions reproduce the causative object's shape, and contusions may not be visible for 24–48 hours — which is why FM14.9 requires photography at intervals for documentation.

answers.text: Incised wound — clean, defined margins from a sharp-edged weapon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incised wounds show disrupted skin with clean margins and no tissue bridges. Intact overlying skin excludes any wound that breaches the surface.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key features here are intact skin + subcutaneous haemorrhage + patterned shape + delayed visibility — all hallmarks of a contusion, not a surface injury or a wound that breaks the skin.

Contusions are unique among mechanical injuries in that they may be invisible initially and develop over 24–48 hours — serial examination and photography are essential for complete medico-legal documentation.
